gancho: Um pilar de ferro de mais de seis toneladas, hoje em Délhi, resiste à ferrugem há uns 1.600 anos, graças, ao que tudo indica, ao fósforo do ferro antigo. Erich von Däniken já o atribuiu a extraterrestres.
explicacao: O pilar, com 7,21 metros de altura, foi feito no tempo do rei Chandragupta II, da dinastia Gupta, que reinou por volta de 375 a 415, e provavelmente ficava em outro lugar antes de ser levado para Délhi. Ele foi produzido soldando a quente pedaços de ferro forjado. Segundo a explicação mais aceita, do metalurgista R. Balasubramaniam, a diferença está na química. Os ferreiros indianos não punham cal nos fornos, enquanto nos altos-fornos modernos o calcário faz a maior parte do fósforo sair junto com a escória. Por isso o ferro do pilar tem bem mais fósforo: em média 0,25%, contra menos de 0,05% no ferro moderno. Com a alternância de umidade e secura do clima, esse fósforo se acumula entre o metal e a ferrugem e acaba virando uma camada contínua de fosfato de ferro cristalino, que protege o metal por baixo. É um processo lento: em 1.600 anos, a película engrossou só um vigésimo de milímetro. No seu primeiro livro, Erich von Däniken citou a falta de corrosão do pilar como prova de visitas extraterrestres. Em 1974, quando um entrevistador lhe disse que o pilar não era livre de ferrugem e que se sabia como ele tinha sido feito, Däniken respondeu que não o considerava mais um mistério.

fontes.trecho: The iron pillar of Delhi is a metal structure 7.21 metres (23 feet 8 inches) high with a 41-centimetre (16 in) diameter that was constructed by Chandragupta II (reigned c. 375–415 CE), and now stands in the Qutb complex at Mehrauli in Delhi, India. The metals used in its construction have a rust-resistant composition. The pillar weighs more than six tonnes and is thought to have been erected elsewhere [...] The pillar was produced by the forge welding of pieces of wrought iron. [...] The ancient Indian smiths did not add lime to their furnaces. In modern blast furnaces, the use of limestone yields pig iron that is later converted into steel; in this process, most phosphorus is carried away by the slag. The absence of lime in the slag and the use of specific quantities of wood with high phosphorus content (for example, Cassia auriculata) during the smelting induces a higher phosphorus content (> 0.1%, average 0.25%) than in modern iron produced in blast furnaces (usually less than 0.05%). [...] Alternate environmental wetting and drying cycles provide the moisture for phosphoric-acid formation. [...] The crystalline phosphate eventually forms a continuous layer next to the metal, which results in an excellent corrosion resistance layer. In 1,600 years, the film has grown just one-twentieth of a millimetre thick. In 1969, in his first book, Chariots of the Gods?, Erich von Däniken cited the absence of corrosion on the Delhi pillar and the unknown nature of its creation as evidence of extraterrestrial visitation. When informed by an interviewer, in 1974, that the column was not in fact rust-free, and that its method of construction was well-understood, von Däniken responded that he no longer considered the pillar or its creation to be a mystery. [...] In a report published in the journal Current Science, R. Balasubramaniam of IIT Kanpur explains how the pillar's resistance to corrosion is due to a passive protective film at the iron-rust interface.

gancho: Os éditos que o imperador indiano Ashoka gravou em pedra no século III a.C. ficaram ilegíveis por séculos. Decifrados entre 1836 e 1838, vinham assinados por "Piyadasi", que o decifrador tomou por um rei do Sri Lanka.
explicacao: Ashoka reinou de cerca de 269 a 233 a.C. e espalhou pelo império textos sobre o "dhamma", uma ética de boas ações, respeito e generosidade. Um deles anuncia tratamento médico para pessoas e também para o gado. A maioria foi escrita nas escritas brahmi e kharoshthi, que se extinguiram por volta do século V d.C. Quando os britânicos estudaram os éditos no século XIX, ninguém sabia lê-los. Em 1836, o norueguês Christian Lassen identificou algumas letras do brahmi graças a moedas bilíngues, em grego e brahmi, de um rei indo-grego. James Prinsep, funcionário da Companhia das Índias Orientais e editor da revista da Sociedade Asiática de Bengala, completou o alfabeto em artigos publicados entre 1836 e 1838. O autor se apresentava como "Devanampriya Piyadasi", "amado dos deuses", e Prinsep primeiro supôs que fosse um rei do Sri Lanka. Só com textos em páli enviados do Sri Lanka ele ligou o título a Ashoka. A confirmação veio em 1915, quando um engenheiro britânico de minas de ouro achou em Maski, no sul da Índia, uma inscrição com o título e o nome de Ashoka juntos. Prinsep, nascido em 1799, começou a sofrer de dores de cabeça e mal-estar em 1838, voltou doente para a Inglaterra e morreu em 1840; diz-se que literalmente se matou de trabalhar.

fontes.trecho: In these inscriptions, Ashoka refers to himself as "Beloved of the Gods" (Devanampiya). The identification of Devanampiya with Ashoka was confirmed by an inscription discovered in 1915 by C. Beadon, a British gold-mining engineer, at Maski, a town in Madras Presidency (present day Raichur district, Karnataka). [...] Besides a few inscriptions in Greek and Aramaic (which were discovered only in the 20th century), the Edicts were mostly written in the Brahmi script and sometimes in the Kharoshthi script in the northwest, two Indian scripts which had both become extinct around the 5th century CE, and were yet undeciphered at the time the Edicts were discovered and investigated in the 19th century. The first successful attempts at deciphering the ancient Brahmi script were made in 1836 by Norwegian scholar Christian Lassen, who used the bilingual Greek-Brahmi coins of Indo-Greek king Agathocles to correctly and securely identify several Brahmi letters. [...] The edicts in Brahmi script mentioned a King Devanampriya Piyadasi which Prinsep initially assumed was a Sri Lankan king. He was then able to associate this title with Ashoka on the basis of Pali script from Sri Lanka communicated to him by George Turnour. [...] Minor Rock Edicts of Ashoka (r.269-233 BCE) [...] two kinds of medical treatment were established by King Devanampriya Priyadarsin, (viz.) medical treatment for men and medical treatment for cattle. [...] is explained mainly in term of moral precepts, based on the doing of good deeds, respect for others, generosity and purity.

James Prinsep  (20 August 1799 – 22 April 1840) was an English scholar, orientalist, and antiquary. He was the founding editor of the Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal and is best remembered for deciphering the Kharosthi and Brahmi scripts of ancient India. [...] Brahmi was deciphered by Prinsep, who was then the secretary of the Society, in a series of scholarly articles published in the Society's journal between 1836 and 1838. [...] Prinsep literally worked himself to death. [...] From 1838 he began to suffer from recurrent headaches and sickness. [...] He arrived in England in poor condition and did not recover.

gancho: Os concursos públicos britânicos se inspiraram em parte nos exames da China imperial. Quando a ideia chegou ao Parlamento, em 1853, um lorde a atacou por ser chinesa, de um país que não seria "esclarecido".
explicacao: Na China, exames sobre os clássicos escolheram funcionários do Estado por cerca de 1.300 anos, até serem abolidos em 1905. Os candidatos ficavam isolados em celas e eram revistados atrás de colas. Mesmo assim, o Minneapolis Institute of Arts guarda uma cola da dinastia Qing: um lenço com 10 mil caracteres dos clássicos confucianos em letra microscópica. Relatos de missionários e diplomatas levaram a ideia ao Ocidente. Em 1806, a Companhia Britânica das Índias Orientais abriu perto de Londres uma escola para seus administradores na Índia, seguindo recomendações de funcionários que tinham visto os exames na China, e em 1829 passou a usar exames, de forma limitada, na Índia. Stafford Northcote, que preparou o relatório que impulsionou o serviço público britânico, conhecia a história e as instituições chinesas. No Parlamento, Lord Monteagle se opôs aos exames abertos por serem um sistema chinês, e Lord Stanley os chamou de "princípio chinês". Os concursos foram adotados no serviço civil britânico da Índia em 1855 e na Inglaterra em 1870. Dez anos depois de aprovados, ainda havia quem os atacasse como "cultura chinesa adotada". Quanto a China de fato pesou na reforma ainda é discutido: ela também respondia à antiga distribuição de cargos por apadrinhamento.

fontes.trecho: The system lasted for 1,300 years until its abolition during the late Qing dynasty reforms in 1905. [...] Guards verified a student's identity and searched him for hidden texts such as cheat sheets. The facilities provided for the examinee consisted of an isolated room or cell with a makeshift bed, desk, and bench. [...] The Minneapolis Institute of Arts holds an example of a Qing dynasty cheatsheet, a handkerchief with 10,000 characters of Confucian classics in microscopically small handwriting. [...] In addition to Asia, reports by European missionaries and diplomats introduced the Chinese examination system to the Western world and encouraged France, Germany and the British East India Company (EIC) to use similar methods to select prospective employees. [...] In 1806, the British East India Company established a Civil Service College near London for training of the company's administrators in India. This was based on the recommendations of East India Company officials serving in China and had seen the Imperial examinations. In 1829, the company introduced civil service examinations in India on a limited basis. [...] Stafford Northcote, 1st Earl of Iddesleigh, who prepared the Northcote–Trevelyan Report that catalyzed the British civil service, were familiar with Chinese history and institutions. When the report was brought up in parliament in 1853, Lord Monteagle argued against the implementation of open examinations because it was a Chinese system and China was not an "enlightened country". Lord Stanley called the examinations the "Chinese Principle". [...] finally implemented in the British Indian Civil Service in 1855, prior to which admission into the civil service was purely a matter of patronage, and in England in 1870. Even as late as ten years after the competitive examination plan was passed, people still attacked it as an "adopted Chinese culture".

gancho: Em Angkor, capital khmer, só os deuses moravam em pedra: até a residência do rei era de madeira. Por isso sobraram os templos, e foram precisas imagens de satélite para revelar uma cidade de pelo menos 1.000 km².
explicacao: Os templos de Angkor, no atual Camboja, são famosos. O maior, Angkor Wat, foi erguido entre 1113 e 1150 pelo rei Suryavarman II. Mas eles eram só a parte duradoura de cidades enormes. No período angkoriano, todos os prédios não religiosos, inclusive a residência do próprio rei, eram feitos de materiais perecíveis, como a madeira, "porque só os deuses tinham direito a residências de pedra". Quase todas as inscrições em pedra que restaram também tratam de fundações religiosas, e por isso é mais fácil contar a história da religião oficial do que a da vida comum. Em 2007, uma equipe internacional usou fotos de satélite e outras técnicas modernas e concluiu que Angkor foi, em área, a maior cidade pré-industrial do mundo: estradas e canais ligavam uma mancha urbana de pelo menos 1.000 km², maior que a Paris de hoje. Mais tarde, o lidar ajudou a achar estruturas escondidas na floresta densa. A rede de reservatórios e canais, que deu a Angkor o apelido de "cidade hidráulica", provavelmente servia para irrigar os campos diante das monções imprevisíveis, embora alguns estudiosos vejam nos grandes reservatórios também um símbolo religioso. O tamanho da população ainda é debatido, mas a agricultura da região pode ter sustentado de 750 mil a 1 milhão de pessoas.

fontes.trecho: In Angkorian times, all non-religious buildings, including the residence of the king himself, were constructed with perishable materials, such as wood, "because only the gods had a right to residences made of stone". Similarly, the vast majority of the surviving stone inscriptions are about the religious foundations of kings and other potentates. As a result, it is easier to write the history of Angkorian state religion than it is to write th [...] In 2007, an international team of researchers using satellite photographs and other modern techniques concluded that Angkor had been the largest pre-industrial city in the world by surface area, with an elaborate infrastructure system connecting an urban sprawl of at least 1,000 square kilometres (390 sq mi). [...] Angkor was considered to be a "hydraulic city" because it had a complicated water management network, which was used for systematically stabilizing, storing, and dispersing water throughout the area. This network is believed to have been used for irrigation in order to offset the unpredictable monsoon season and to also support the increasing population. Although the size of its population remains a topic of research and debate, newly identified agricultural systems in the Angkor area may have supported between 750,000 and 1,000,000 people. [...] At its peak, the city occupied an area greater than modern Paris [...] The single largest temple of the Angkorian region, Angkor Wat, was built between 1113 and 1150 by King Suryavarman II. [...] archaeologists have used LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging)  to uncover structures such as building rods, monuments, and other features. This was beneficial for archaeologists to use because of Angkor's location. Some of the site, is in dense forest [...] The significance of such reservoirs has been debated by modern scholars, some believing the use was the irrigation of rice fields,  others have regarded them as religiously charged symbols of the great mythological oceans surrounding Mount Meru, the abode of the gods.

gancho: O mais antigo grande conjunto de escrita chinesa, gravado em ossos e cascos de tartaruga há mais de três mil anos, era vendido como "ossos de dragão" e moído para virar remédio. Ninguém sabe quantos foram engolidos.
explicacao: No fim da dinastia Shang, por volta de 1250 a 1050 a.C., adivinhos gravavam perguntas aos deuses em omoplatas de boi e cascos de tartaruga: sobre o tempo, o plantio, a sorte da família real, as guerras. Depois aqueciam a peça com uma haste de metal até ela rachar e liam a resposta no desenho das rachaduras. No século XIX, camponeses que cavavam os campos na região acharam esses ossos e os usaram como "ossos de dragão", seguindo a prática da medicina tradicional de moer fósseis para fazer tônicos e emplastros. Os cascos eram receitados contra malária, e os outros ossos, em pó, para cortes de faca. Em 1899, um antiquário vendeu alguns a Wang Yirong, chanceler da Academia Imperial em Pequim e colecionador de bronzes antigos. Ele é tido como o primeiro, nos tempos modernos, a reconhecer nos traços uma escrita chinesa antiga. Uma história lendária diz que ele os achou entre os próprios remédios, quando estava com malária. Hoje se conhecem cerca de 13 mil ossos, com pouco mais de 130 mil inscrições, e eles confirmaram a existência da dinastia Shang, então posta em dúvida por uma escola de historiadores. Como observou uma estudiosa, não há como saber quantos desses ossos as farmácias moeram antes de 1899.

fontes.trecho: Oracle bones are pieces of ox scapula and turtle plastron which were used in pyromancy – a form of divination – during the Late Shang period (c. 1250 – c. 1050 BCE) in ancient China. [...] A recent count estimated that there were about 13,000 bones with a total of a little over 130,000 inscriptions in collections in China and some fourteen other countries. Diviners would submit questions to deities regarding weather, crop planting, the fortunes of members of the royal family, military endeavors, and similar topics. [...] Intense heat was then applied with a metal rod until the bone or shell cracked due to thermal expansion. The diviner would then interpret the pattern of cracks [...] Oracle bones bear the earliest known significant corpus of ancient Chinese writing [...] these records confirmed the existence of the Shang, whose historicity had been subject to scrutiny at the time by the Doubting Antiquity School. [...] During the 19th century, villagers in the area who were digging in the fields discovered a number of bones, and used them as dragon bones, following the traditional Chinese medicine practice of grinding up Pleistocene fossils into tonics or poultices. The turtle shell fragments were prescribed for malaria, while the other animal bones were used in powdered form to treat knife wounds. In 1899, an antiques dealer from Shandong who was searching for Chinese bronzes in the area acquired a number of oracle bones from locals, and later sold several to Wang Yirong, the chancellor of the Imperial Academy in Beijing.  Wang was a knowledgeable collector of Chinese bronzes, and is believed to be the first person in modern times to recognize the oracle bones' markings as ancient Chinese writing similar to that on Zhou dynasty bronzes. A legendary tale relates that Wang was sick with malaria, and his scholar friend Liu E was visiting him and helped examine his medicine. [...] Xu Yahui states that, "[n]o one can know how many oracle bones, prior to 1899, were ground up by traditional Chinese pharmacies and disappeared into people's stomachs."

gancho: Uma nobre chinesa morta há mais de dois mil anos foi achada com pele macia, juntas que dobravam, restos de sangue nas veias e mais de 130 sementes de melão no aparelho digestivo. Não se sabe bem como se conservou.
explicacao: Xin Zhui, a marquesa de Dai, morreu com cerca de 50 anos, por volta de 168 a.C., durante a dinastia Han Ocidental. O túmulo, em Mawangdui, perto de Changsha, foi achado por operários que cavavam um abrigo antiaéreo para um hospital. O corpo estava envolto em vinte camadas de roupa, dentro de quatro caixões encaixados, enterrados sob camadas de carvão e argila branca. A conservação permitiu uma autópsia em dezembro de 1972: os órgãos e os vasos estavam intactos, com um pouco de sangue tipo A, e os cílios e as impressões digitais estavam nítidos. Ela tinha arteriosclerose, cálculos biliares e um parasita, a esquistossomose, e morreu de um ataque cardíaco. As mais de 130 sementes de melão no estômago, no intestino e no esôfago indicam que ela morreu duas a três horas depois de comer a fruta, provavelmente no verão. O caixão continha um líquido ácido, com sal e magnésio, que pode ter impedido as bactérias de crescer; o contato com ele deu nos cientistas da autópsia uma irritação nas mãos que durou três meses. Mas os cientistas não sabem exatamente qual combinação de fatores a preservou, nem por que condições quase iguais falharam com outros corpos, que viraram esqueleto ou pó em caixões também herméticos.

fontes.trecho: c. 217 BC – 169 or 168 BC), also known as Lady Dai or the Marchioness of Dai, was a Chinese noblewoman. [...] during the Western Han dynasty. [...] she also had coronary thrombosis and arteriosclerosis [...] She also suffered from gallstones [...] eventually led to a heart attack that caused her death. Along with schistosomiasis, a parasitic infection [...] A total of 130 melon seeds were found in Xin Zhui's stomach, intestines, and esophagus; researchers believed she consumed the melon very quickly. From this, researchers inferred that she died in summer, when fruits and melons ripen. The presence of melon seeds in her stomach also indicates that she died within two to three hours of eating the fruit. Xin Zhui died at approximately 50 years of age in 169 or 168 BC. [...] workers digging an air raid shelter for a hospital near Changsha unearthed the tomb of Xin Zhui [...] Xin Zhui's body was found within four rectangular pine constructs that sat inside one another which were buried beneath layers of charcoal and white clay. The corpse was wrapped in twenty layers of clothing bound with silk ribbons. [...] Her skin was soft and moist, with muscles that still allowed for her arms and legs to flex at the joints. All her organs and blood vessels were also intact, with small amounts of Type A blood being found in her veins. [...] her eyelashes and nose hair remained intact. The tympanic membrane of her left ear was also intact, and her finger and toe prints were distinct. This preservation allowed doctors at Hunan Provincial Medical Institute to perform an autopsy on 14 December 1972. [...] The mysterious liquid she was soaked in was acidic, which may have worked to preserve the body by preventing bacteria from growing. Tests revealed it to also contain salt and magnesium. [...] When the autopsy on Xin Zhui's remains was done, contact with the fluid caused a rash on the hands of the scientists conducting it. The rash persisted on their skin for three months. [...] However, scientists do not know for certain what combination of factors helped preserve Xin Zhui's corpse, or why almost the same conditions failed to preserve other bodies. [...] In addition, similar airtight and watertight coffins failed to keep other cadavers from decomposing into skeletons or dust.

gancho: No túmulo de um marquês chinês de cerca de 433 a.C. havia 64 sinos de bronze afinados, e cada um toca duas notas, conforme o ponto em que é golpeado. Séculos depois, os sinos chineses passaram a dar uma nota só.
explicacao: O túmulo do marquês Yi, que governou Zeng, um pequeno Estado sob o domínio do reino de Chu, foi achado por acaso pelo Exército de Libertação Popular, que derrubava um morro para erguer uma fábrica. É um dos poucos túmulos reais chineses antigos encontrados intactos e escavados com métodos modernos. Na câmara central estava um grande conjunto de bianzhong, sinos de bronze pendurados numa armação, golpeados com malhos de madeira por cinco músicos e cobrindo cinco oitavas. Cada sino dá um tom quando é golpeado no centro e outro quando é golpeado na lateral. O truque está no formato: a seção do sino não é redonda, e sim em forma de amêndoa. Inscrições nos sinos registram a relação entre os padrões de afinação de Zeng, de Chu e da dinastia Zhou. Mais tarde, nas dinastias Qin e Tang, a construção mudou: os conjuntos ficaram menores e cada sino passou a produzir uma única nota. O túmulo guardava também os restos de oito mulheres na câmara do marquês e de outras treze numa câmara a oeste. Desde a escavação, o conjunto só foi tocado três vezes, a última na cerimônia de devolução de Hong Kong à China, em 1997.

fontes.titulo: Tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng
fontes.trecho: is one of a handful of ancient Chinese royal tombs to have been discovered intact and then excavated using modern archaeological methods. [...] The tomb was made around 433 BC [...] The People's Liberation Army accidentally discovered the tomb in 1977 while destroying a hill to build a factory at Leigudun. [...] The eastern chamber contained the tomb of Marquis Yi, who was buried in a wooden lacquer coffin nested inside a larger lacquer coffin. This chamber also contained eight other coffins that held the remains of eight women. The western chamber contained thirteen coffins that held the remains of thirteen other women. The central chamber is the largest, and contained a large ensemble of ritual musical instruments, including a set of 64 bianzhong (bronze bells). [...] The most famous discovery at the tomb is the large set of 64 bianzhong bells, mounted on an elaborate framework, which required a cast of five members to be played, and were struck with wooden mallets to produce music. The bells are two-toned, producing two distinct tones when struck at the center or the side. This property is due to the bells' almond-shaped cross-section. The bells cover a range of five octaves. [...] The bells were inscribed with music notations that detailed the relationship among the pitch standards of Zeng, Chu and Zhou.

The instrument's construction shifted dramatically in the Qin and Tang dynasties (221 BC – 907 CE). bianzhong decreased in size during this period, being limited to sets of 14, 16, and 24 bells. Due to differences in bell construction, each zhong produced only one pitch. [...] Yi was the ruler of Zeng, one of the minor states under control of the major State of Chu. [...] has been performed on three times since its excavation in 1978, the most recent being for the Hong Kong Reunification ceremony in 1997.

gancho: Em 1819, um oficial britânico que caçava tigres na Índia foi levado por um pastorzinho às cavernas budistas de Ajanta, cheias de pinturas antigas. Lá dentro, riscou de propósito o nome sobre a figura de um bodisatva.
explicacao: As 30 cavernas de Ajanta, mosteiros e salões de culto escavados na rocha entre o século II a.C. e cerca de 480 d.C., incluem, nas cavernas 1, 2, 16 e 17, o maior conjunto de pinturas murais da Índia antiga que chegou até nós. Elas não eram segredo para os moradores da região e aparecem até em memórias de viajantes budistas chineses da Idade Média, mas estavam cobertas pela mata. Em 28 de abril de 1819, John Smith, da 28ª Cavalaria, foi guiado por um pastorzinho até a entrada da caverna 10. Chamou aldeões com machados, lanças, tochas e tambores para abrir caminho na vegetação, viu tetos com rostos pintados, percebeu que se tratava de um mosteiro budista e então riscou o seu nome e a data sobre a pintura de um bodisatva. Como estava de pé sobre um monte de entulho de cinco pés de altura, a inscrição ficou bem acima dos olhos de quem visita o lugar hoje. As cópias das pinturas também tiveram azar. Das 27 que o major Robert Gill pintou ali, todas menos quatro queimaram num incêndio no Palácio de Cristal, em Londres, em 1866. Em 1885, outro incêndio destruiu mais de cem telas de uma segunda equipe, guardadas num museu.

fontes.trecho: The Ajanta Caves are 30 rock-cut Buddhist cave monuments dating from the second century BCE to about 480 CE in Aurangabad district of Maharashtra state in India. [...] The Ajanta Caves constitute ancient monasteries (Viharas) and worship-halls (Chaityas) of different Buddhist traditions carved into a 75-metre (246 ft) wall of rock. [...] Caves 1, 2, 16 and 17 of Ajanta form the largest corpus of surviving ancient Indian wall-paintings. The Ajanta Caves are mentioned in the memoirs of several medieval-era Chinese Buddhist travelers. They were covered by the jungle until accidentally "discovered" and brought to contemporary attention in 1819 by Colonel John Smith during a tiger-hunting expedition [...] On 28 April 1819 a British officer named John Smith, of the 28th Cavalry, while hunting tigers was shown the entrance to Cave No. 10 when a local shepherd boy guided him to the location and the door. The caves were well known by locals already. Captain Smith went to a nearby village and asked the villagers to come to the site with axes, spears, torches, and drums, to cut down the tangled jungle growth that made entering the cave difficult. He first saw ceilings with beautiful and artistically drawn faces on them, then he noticed monastic halls which helped him identify their Buddhist origin. He then deliberately damaged an image on the wall by scratching his name and the date over the painting of a bodhisattva. Since he stood on a five-foot high pile of rubble collected over the years, the inscription is well above the eye-level gaze of an adult today. [...] He made 27 copies of large sections of murals, but all but four were destroyed in a fire at the Crystal Palace in London in 1866, where they were on display. [...] But in 1885 another fire destroyed over a hundred of the paintings in storage in a wing of the museum.

gancho: Desde cerca de 256 a.C., um sistema de irrigação na China controla as cheias do rio Min sem represá-lo: um dique em forma de boca de peixe divide a água e manda mais para as lavouras na seca e menos na cheia.
explicacao: O rio Min descia das montanhas cheio do degelo da primavera, perdia velocidade na planície de Chengdu, acumulava sedimento e transbordava. Li Bing, hidrólogo do Estado de Qin, podia ter feito uma barragem, mas Qin queria manter o rio aberto para os barcos militares que abasteciam as tropas na fronteira. A solução foi desviar parte do fluxo com um dique feito de cestos compridos de bambu trançado cheios de pedras. O dique "boca de peixe" separa um braço interno, fundo e estreito, de um braço externo, raso e largo. Na estação seca, o braço interno leva cerca de 60% da água para a irrigação; na cheia, a fatia cai para 40%, e o braço externo leva embora boa parte do sedimento. Faltava abrir um canal na montanha, numa época anterior à pólvora. Li Bing aquecia a rocha com fogo e a esfriava com água até ela rachar, e depois de oito anos havia um corte de 20 metros de largura. Degradado nas convulsões do século XVII e destruído por um terremoto em 1933, o sistema foi reconstruído e ainda irriga mais de 5.300 km². Desde 2000, é Patrimônio Mundial da Unesco.

fontes.trecho: Originally constructed around 256 BC by the State of Qin as an irrigation and flood control project, it is still in use today. [...] Originally, the Min would rush down from the Min Mountains and slow down abruptly after reaching the Chengdu Plain, filling the watercourse with silt, thus making the nearby areas extremely prone to floods. King Zhao of Qin commissioned the project, and the construction of the Dujiangyan harnessed the river using a new method of channeling and dividing the water rather than simply damming it. The water management scheme is still in use today to irrigate over 5,300 km2 (2,000 sq mi) of land in the region [...] Dujiangyan Irrigation System was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2000. [...] Qin hydrologist Li Bing investigated the problem and discovered that the river was swelled by fast flowing spring melt-water from the local mountains that burst the banks when it reached the slow moving and heavily silted stretch below. One solution would have been to build a dam, but the Qin wanted to keep the waterway open for military vessels to supply troops on the frontier, so instead an artificial levee was constructed to redirect a portion of the river's flow [...] The levee was constructed from long sausage-shaped baskets of woven bamboo filled with stones known as Zhulong [...] Cutting the channel proved to be a far greater problem, as the hand tools available at the time, prior to the invention of gunpowder, would have taken decades to cut through the mountain. Li Bing devised an ingenious method of using fire and water to rapidly heat and cool the rocks, causing them to crack and allowing them to be easily removed. After eight years of work, a channel 20 meters (66 ft) wide had been gouged through the mountain. [...] The original Dujiangyan irrigation system was destroyed by the 1933 Diexi earthquake. The current Dujiangyan irrigation system was rebuilt after the Diexi earthquake in 1933 [...] It is an artificial levee that divides the water into inner and outer streams. The inner stream is deep and narrow, while the outer stream is relatively shallow but wide. This special structure ensures that the inner stream carries approximately 60% of the river's flow into the irrigation system during dry season. While during flood, this amount decreases to 40% to protect the people from flooding. The outer stream drains away the rest, flushing out much of the silt and sediment. [...] Turmoil surrounding the conquering of Chengdu by peasant rebel leader Zhang Xianzhong in 1644, and the Ming-Qing transition more generally, led to depopulation and the deterioration of the Dujiangyan irrigation system to the point where rice cultivation was set back for decades.

gancho: O maior túmulo do Japão, um monte de cerca de 500 metros, é atribuído ao imperador Nintoku, mas não há como confirmar: ele fica sob a guarda da Casa Imperial, que restringe o acesso até de arqueólogos.
explicacao: Entre meados do século III e o início do século VIII, o Japão ergueu cerca de 160 mil kofun, montes de terra e pedra sobre túmulos da elite. Os maiores têm formato de buraco de fechadura. O de Daisen, em Sakai, perto de Osaka, é o maior do país: cercado por três fossos, teria levado uns 20 anos para ser construído, em meados do século V, e estima-se que o monte tenha sido coberto por cerca de 50 milhões de pedras. Boa parte das atribuições de túmulos a imperadores vem do século XIX. Depois da restauração do poder imperial, em 1868, o governo atribuiu muitos túmulos a personagens das crônicas Kojiki e Nihon Shoki, do início do século VIII, e, como o imperador era tido como divino, eles ganharam caráter sagrado. Depois da derrota de 1945, os cerca de 900 túmulos atribuídos a ancestrais imperiais passaram à Agência da Casa Imperial como túmulos privados, e o acesso continuou proibido, decisão cercada de polêmica. Ficam perguntas sem resposta: quem está enterrado ali? Os túmulos teriam provas de uma ascendência coreana da família imperial? Mesmo com sinais oficiais recentes de abertura, quase ninguém de fora da agência consegue entrar. O monte está tomado pela vegetação, e os fossos viraram refúgio de peixes e aves aquáticas.

fontes.trecho: The Daisenryo Kofun (大仙陵古墳, Daisenryō kofun), the largest kofun in Japan, is believed to have been constructed over a period of 20 years in the mid 5th century during the Kofun Period.  While it cannot be accurately confirmed, it is commonly accepted that the tomb was built for the late Emperor Nintoku. The Imperial Household Agency of Japan treats it as such. [...] In the Japanese archipelago, more than 20,000 tumuli (kofun), which are mounds of earth and stones erected over graves of the ruling class, were built between the later part of the 3rd century and the 6th century. [...] The larger ones are keyhole-shaped (zempō kōenfun) [...] The Daisen Kofun mound is approximately 500 metres (1,600 ft) long and 300 metres (980 ft) across at its widest point, while the entire tomb area is 840 metres (2,760 ft) long. Enclosed by three moats [...] Today, the tomb is off-limits and protected by the Imperial Household Agency in the centre of Sakai City.  The moats have been maintained and provide a sanctuary for fish and waterbirds.  The mound itself is completely overgrown by vegetation.

fontes.titulo: Japan's royal tombs: Burial mounds and Korean connections in the 3rd-8th centuries AD (Current World Archaeology, 2024)
fontes.trecho: following the restoration of imperial power in 1868, the Japanese government assigned many tombs to personages mentioned in ancient chronicles, specifically the Kojiki ('Records of Ancient Matters') dating to 712 and the Nihon Shoki ('Chronicles of Japan') drawn up in 720. As the emperor was regarded as divine, these tombs took on special sacred significance. Following Japan's defeat in 1945, and the Showa Emperor's renunciation of his divinity, the 900 or so tombs attributed to imperial ancestors came into the guardianship of the Imperial Household Agency as private graves. Access to them continued to be forbidden, a decision around which controversy has swirled. Many questions remain, such as who was buried within? Do the tombs contain proof that the Japanese imperial family was in fact of Korean descent? [...] Despite recent official statements suggesting some change in policy, access continues to be largely denied to anyone beyond the Imperial Household Agency. [...] It is estimated that some 160,000 burial mounds (kofun in Japanese, meaning ‘old mound’) were constructed between the middle of the 3rd century AD and the early 8th century.

fontes.titulo: Archaeologists Investigate Japan's Daisen Kofun (Archaeology, 27 nov. 2018)
fontes.trecho: is thought to have been built in the mid-fifth century A.D. for Emperor Nintoku. Little is known about the structure, however, because in the past access to it has been limited by Japan's Imperial Household Agency. Scholars think the mound itself was covered with some 50 million stones.

gancho: Em 1986, operários na China acharam covas com milhares de objetos de ouro, bronze e jade, quebrados, queimados e enterrados com cuidado. A cultura que os fez tinha um estilo desconhecido e não deixou registros escritos.
explicacao: O sítio de Sanxingdui, na província de Sichuan, tem peças datadas por radiocarbono dos séculos XII e XI a.C. Elas são da mesma época da dinastia Shang, mas num estilo de bronze bem diferente, e os pesquisadores se espantaram com uma arte totalmente desconhecida na história chinesa. Há dezenas de grandes máscaras e cabeças de bronze com olhos amendoados exagerados, algumas com as pupilas saltadas para fora, e orelhas enormes. Há também a estátua humana de pé, em tamanho natural, mais antiga do mundo, com 260 centímetros, e uma árvore de bronze de 396 centímetros, com pássaros e flores. As peças foram quebradas, talvez de propósito, num ritual, depois queimadas e enterradas. Há pistas: crônicas compiladas mais de mil anos depois dizem que o fundador do reino de Shu, Cancong, tinha olhos saltados, como as máscaras, mas há outras interpretações. Sem registros escritos, é difícil saber para que serviam os objetos, e o fim dessa cultura também é debatido: desastres naturais, com sinais de grandes enchentes e de um terremoto, ou a invasão de outro povo. Seis novas covas, escavadas entre 2020 e 2022, renderam mais peças, entre elas uma máscara de ouro.

fontes.trecho: Largely discovered in 1986, following a preliminary finding in 1927, archaeologists excavated artifacts that radiocarbon dating placed in the 12th–11th centuries BC. [...] According to the Chronicles of Huayang that were compiled during the Jin dynasty (266–420), the Shu kingdom was founded by Cancong (蠶叢). Cancong was described as having protruding eyes, a feature that is found in many of the masks and figures of Sanxingdui. It has therefore been suggested that the large masks with protruding eyes are a representation of Cancong, although there are other interpretations. [...] In 1986, local workers accidentally found sacrificial pits containing thousands of gold, bronze, jade, and pottery artifacts that had been broken (perhaps ritually disfigured), burned, and carefully buried. [...] Researchers  were astonished to find an artistic style that was completely unknown in the history of Chinese art. [...] The six pits were discovered at the Sanxingdui site between 2020 and 2022 during a renewed slate of excavations. The artifacts found in these excavations include fragments of a gold mask [...] This culture is contemporaneous with the Shang dynasty, but it developed a different artistic style of bronze-making from the Shang. [...] Speculation regarding the end of the Sanxingdui culture includes that it might have been the result of natural disasters (evidence of massive flooding and an earthquake were found), or invasion by another culture. [...] such as the world's oldest life-sized standing human statue (260 centimetres [100 in] high, 180 kilograms (400 lb)), and a bronze tree with birds, flowers, and ornaments (396 centimetres [156 in]) [...] The most striking finds were dozens of large bronze masks and heads (at least six heads with gold foil masks originally attached) represented with angular human features, exaggerated almond-shaped eyes, some with protruding pupils, and large upper ears. [...] As no written records remain it is difficult to determine the intended uses of objects found.

gancho: Livros de sucesso dizem que a rebelião de An Lushan, na China do século VIII, matou 36 milhões de pessoas. O número sai de dois censos, e muitos historiadores acham que ele mede sobretudo o colapso do próprio censo.
explicacao: A rebelião, uma guerra civil contra a dinastia Tang, durou de 755 a 763, chegou a tomar a capital, Chang'an, e despovoou regiões com fome, fugas e destruição. O último censo antes dela, de 755, registrou 52.919.309 pessoas. O de 764, logo depois do fim da guerra, registrou só 16,9 milhões. A diferença, uns 36 milhões, dois terços da população do império, entrou no livro "The Better Angels of Our Nature", de Steven Pinker, como a maior atrocidade da história em proporção, um sexto da população mundial da época, embora o próprio Pinker dissesse que o número era controverso. Matthew White, de quem Pinker tirou a estimativa, depois a revisou para 13 milhões. Historiadores como Charles Patrick Fitzgerald lembram que a guerra foi travada, com interrupções, em três ou quatro províncias. Para eles, os registros do pós-guerra refletem também a perda de precisão do sistema, a retirada da contagem de grupos que não pagavam imposto, como religiosos, estrangeiros e mercadores, e o fato de que províncias do norte, com cerca de um quarto da população, deixaram de prestar contas ao fisco. Em 1947, Hans Bielenstein escreveu que só uma crença "comicamente ingênua" na sede de sangue dos combatentes levaria a ler aquela queda como mortes.

fontes.trecho: The An Lushan rebellion was a civil war in China that lasted from 755 to 763, at the approximate midpoint of the Tang dynasty (618–907). [...] The rebels succeeded in capturing the imperial capital Chang'an [...] the military activities and associated casualties caused significant depopulation from famine, displacement, and large-scale infrastructure destruction [...] the last census undertaken before the rebellion, in 755, recording a population of 52,919,309 in 8,914,709 taxpaying households. However, a census taken in 764, the year following the end of the rebellion, recorded only 16,900,000 in 2,900,000 households. [...] The difference in the census figures amounts to 36 million people fewer, two-thirds of the population of the empire, though scholars have attributed this to factors including a breakdown in taxation and census gathering. The figure of 36 million was used in Steven Pinker's book The Better Angels of Our Nature, where it is presented as proportionally the largest atrocity in history with the loss of a sixth of the world's population at that time, though Pinker stated that the figure was controversial. Matthew White, from whom Pinker had taken the figure of 36 million, later revised his figure down to 13 million [...] Historians such as Charles Patrick Fitzgerald argue that claims of massive depopulation are incompatible with contemporary accounts of the war, which was fought intermittently over three or four provinces. They point out that the numbers recorded on the postwar registers reflect not only population loss, but also a breakdown of accuracy of the census system as well as the removal from the census figures of various classes of untaxed persons, such as those in religious orders, foreigners and merchants. In addition, several of the northern provinces, with approximately a quarter of the empire's population, were no longer subject to the imperial revenue system. [...] In 1947, Hans Bielenstein likewise criticized the conclusions drawn by earlier scholars from rebellion-era censuses, stating: "One must have a comically naive belief in the fighting parties' bestiality and bloodthirst to assert that An Lu-shan's rebellion in 755 should have reduced the population of China from 51.6 million people to 17 million."

gancho: Os guardiões musculosos e furiosos nos portões de templos budistas do Japão teriam um ancestral grego: Héracles. Na arte greco-budista, o herói virou o protetor do Buda, e essa imagem viajou pelo Leste Asiático.
explicacao: O protetor em questão é Vajrapani, nome sânscrito que significa "com o raio (ou o diamante) na mão". Quando o budismo se espalhou pela Ásia Central e se misturou a influências helenísticas, no chamado greco-budismo, o herói grego Héracles foi adotado para representá-lo: um atleta musculoso e peludo, com uma clava curta. Na arte de Gandhara, durante o Império Kushan, Vajrapani aparece sobretudo como protetor de Sakyamuni, o Buda histórico. Há autores que veem nessas imagens não Héracles, mas Zeus, cujo atributo clássico é justamente o raio. De todo modo, a figura de Vajrapani como um lutador forte acabou influenciando as estátuas de divindades guardiãs no Leste Asiático. No Japão, onde ele se chama Shukongōshin, sua imagem inspirou os Niō, os "Reis Benevolentes", os guardiões de expressão feroz e músculos saltados que ficam na entrada de muitos templos budistas. Na China e em Taiwan, formas de Vajrapani também vigiam os portões de templos e mosteiros.

fontes.trecho: As Buddhism expanded in Central Asia and fused with Hellenistic influences into Greco-Buddhism, the Greek hero Heracles was adopted to represent Vajrapāni. In that era, he was typically depicted as a hairy, muscular athlete, wielding a short "diamond" club. [...] Some authors believe that the deity depicted is actually Zeus, whose Classical attribute is the thunderbolt. The image of Vajrapani as a wrestler-like figure would eventually influence the statues of guardian deities in East Asia. [...] During the Kushan Empire, Gandhara art depicted Vajrapani's images in which he is shown primarily as a protector of Sakyamuni and not in the role of a bodhisattva. [...] Manifestations of Vajrapāni can also be found in many Buddhist temples in China, Taiwan and Japan as Dharma protectors guarding monastery and temple gates. [...] In Japan, Vajrapāni is called Shukongōshin (執金剛神), the on'yomi reading of his Chinese name. As in China, his image was the inspiration for the Niō (仁王; Benevolent Kings), the wrath-filled and muscular guardian of the Buddha, found at the entrance of many Buddhist temples. [...] Vajrapāni, "holder of the thunderbolt", is a compound word in Sanskrit in which 'Vajra' means "Diamond or Thunderbolt", and 'pāni' literally means "in hand".

gancho: Em 781, na capital da China Tang, cristãos da Igreja do Oriente ergueram uma estela em chinês e siríaco sobre 150 anos de cristianismo no país. Enterrada em 845, voltou à luz no século XVII, e Voltaire duvidou dela.
explicacao: Segundo a estela, o missionário Alopen chegou em 635, vindo de Daqin, nome chinês para o Império Romano do Oriente, com livros sagrados e imagens, e a Igreja do Oriente foi reconhecida pelo imperador Taizong. O texto, com cerca de 1.900 caracteres chineses e glosas em siríaco, chama Deus de "Verdadeiro Senhor", menciona o Gênesis, a cruz e o batismo e lista uns setenta monges e sacerdotes, alguns com nomes persas. Um deles, Yisi, foi comandante militar na repressão à rebelião de An Lushan, e a corte Tang recompensou a ele e à igreja com títulos e cargos. A pedra foi provavelmente enterrada em 845, durante a perseguição Huichang, voltada ao budismo, mas que também atingiu os cristãos. Desenterrada no fim da dinastia Ming, ela foi traduzida por jesuítas e virou notícia na Europa, onde críticos anticatólicos e antijesuítas disseram que a pedra era falsa ou que os jesuítas tinham mexido no texto. A ideia foi retomada por jansenistas franceses e por Voltaire. Em 1907, o aventureiro dinamarquês Frits Holm foi a Xi'an disposto a levar a estela para a Europa. As autoridades locais o impediram e a transferiram para o museu Floresta de Estelas, onde ela está até hoje. Holm se contentou com uma cópia exata, que mandou para Nova York.

fontes.trecho: is a stele, erected in 781 during the Tang dynasty, that documents approximately 150 years of early Christianity in China. It is a limestone block 279 centimetres (9 ft 2 in) high with text in both Chinese and Syriac describing the existence of Christian communities in several cities in northern China. It reveals that the initial Church of the East had met recognition by the Tang Emperor Taizong, due to efforts of the Christian missionary Alopen in 635. According to the stele, Alopen and his fellow Syriac missionaries came to China from Daqin (the Eastern Roman Empire) in the ninth year of Emperor Taizong (635), bringing sacred books and images. [...] Buried in 845, probably during the Huichang persecution of Buddhism, the stele was not rediscovered until 1625. [...] The stele is thought to have been buried in 845, during the Huichang persecution, which also affected Christians. The stele was unearthed in the late Ming dynasty (between 1621 and 1625) beside Chongren Temple (崇仁寺) outside of Xi'an. [...] The names of several higher clergy (one bishop, two chorepiscopi and two archdeacons) and around seventy monks or priests are listed. [...] Some of the Church of the East monks had distinctive Persian names (such as Isadsafas, Gushnasap), suggesting that they might have come from Fars or elsewhere in Persia [...] Below this headpiece is a long Chinese inscription, consisting of around 1,900 Chinese characters, sometimes glossed in Syriac (several sentences amounting to about 50 Syriac words). Referring to God using the title 真主, Pinyin: Zhēnzhǔ (literally "Veritable Majesty" or "True Lord"), the text refers to Genesis, the cross, and baptism. [...] Yazedbuzid (Yisi in Chinese) helped the Tang dynasty general Guo Ziyi militarily crush the Sogdian-Turk led An Lushan rebellion, with Yisi personally acting as a military commander and Yisi and the Church of the East were rewarded by the Tang dynasty with titles and positions as described in the Xi'an Stele. [...] The Xi'an Stele attracted the attention of some anti-Christian, Protestant anti-Catholic, or Catholic anti-Jesuit groups in the 17th century, who argued that the stone was a fake or that the inscriptions had been modified by the Jesuits who served in the Ming Court. [...] Later, Navarrete's point of view was taken up by French Jansenists and Voltaire. [...] The Danish scholar and adventurer Frits Holm came to Xi'an in 1907 planning to take the monument for himself to Europe. Local authorities prevented him and moved the stele, complete with its tortoise, from its location near Chongren Temple to Xi'an's Beilin Museum (Forest of Steles Museum). Holm had an exact copy of the stele made for him and had the replica stele shipped to New York [...] The original Xi'an Stele remains in the Forest of Steles.

gancho: Uma construtora japonesa fundada em 578 por carpinteiros vindos do reino coreano de Baekje funcionou por mais de 1.400 anos nas mãos de 40 gerações da mesma família. Quando faltava filho, o genro adotava o sobrenome.
explicacao: No século VI, quando o budismo ainda era pouco difundido no Japão, o príncipe Shōtoku encomendou o templo Shitennō-ji, em Osaka, e convidou carpinteiros de Baekje, na Coreia, para liderar a obra. Um dos que trabalharam na construção fundou depois a Kongō Gumi, especializada em templos e santuários. Um pergaminho do século XVII, com 3 metros de comprimento, traça as 40 gerações da família desde a fundação. Como em muitas famílias japonesas de prestígio, os genros entravam no clã e adotavam o nome Kongō, e assim a linhagem seguiu ora por um filho, ora por uma filha. A construção de templos budistas garantiu trabalho constante, e a firma participou de obras como o Castelo de Osaka, do século XVI. Em 1934, quando um tufão derrubou o pagode de cinco andares do Shitennō-ji, a reconstrução foi comandada por Yoshie Kongō, a primeira mulher a chefiar os carpinteiros da empresa. O fim veio com o concreto e as dívidas: a concorrência de grandes construtoras cresceu com o uso de concreto em templos, e em janeiro de 2006 a Kongō Gumi passou a ser subsidiária do grupo Takamatsu. O último presidente da família, Masakazu Kongō, foi o 40º Kongō no comando.

fontes.trecho: é uma construtora japonesa, considerada a mais antiga companhia independente do mundo, que operou por mais de mil e quatrocentos anos até ser adquirida como subsidiária pelo Takamatsu Construction Group em 2006. Com sede em Ósaca, esta empresa familiar foi fundada em 578, quando o príncipe Shōtoku Taishi trouxe vários membros da família Kongō de Baekje ao Japão, para construir o templo budista Shitennō-ji

increased competition from major construction companies due to the growing use of concrete in shrines and temples resulted in the company becoming a subsidiary of the Takamatsu Construction Group in January 2006. [...] A 3-metre-long (9.8 ft) 17th century scroll traces the 40 generations back to the company's start. It has continued operation through the founder's descendants. As with many distinguished Japanese families, sons-in-law often joined the clan and took the Kongō family name. This allowed the company to continue with the same name when there were no sons in a generation. Thus, through the years, the line has continued through either a son or a daughter. Another factor for the company's longevity is the Buddhist temple construction business [...] Kongō Gumi participated in the construction of many famous buildings, including the 16th century Osaka Castle. [...] The last president was Masakazu Kongō, the 40th Kongō to lead the firm. [...] In 1934, the Shitennō-ji Gojū-no-tō (five-story pagoda) collapsed due to the 1934 Muroto typhoon. Kongō Gumi was able to rebuild it under the leadership of Yoshie Kongō, the first woman to become the head carpenter in the company's history. [...] The over-1,400-year-old Kongō family's management structure essentially closed its doors.

Prince Shōtoku was known for his profound Buddhist faith when Buddhism was not widespread in Japan during the 6th century. [...] he commissioned the construction of Shitennō-ji. Prince Shōtoku invited three Korean carpenters from Baekje that brought knowledge and led the construction of Shitennō-ji. [...] One of the members involved in the initial construction of the temple in the 6th century later established the firm Kongō Gumi, which specialized in temple and shrine buildings.
